originalProse: The loop starts at 2 and repeats while n is less than 5, so n takes the values 2, 3 and 4. Each pass adds n to total, which grows from 0 to 2, then 5, then 9.
Arrays count their positions from zero. An array with three elements therefore has indexes 0, 1 and 2, and asking for index 3 gives undefined instead of an error.
Printing inside a function shows a value to the person watching the console, but the code that called the function receives undefined unless a return statement hands the value over.
The condition of a for loop is tested before every pass. As soon as it is false the loop ends, and execution moves on to the first statement after the loop.
Declare the total before the loop, change it inside the loop, and read it after the loop ends. The loop condition decides which values take part.
The last index is always one less than the number of elements in the array, so reading one position further returns undefined.
copiedProse: A counting loop repeats its body while a condition stays true. The counter is checked before each pass, so the moment the condition fails, the body is skipped and the program continues with whatever comes after the closing brace.
A list keeps its entries in the order you added them, and every entry sits at a numbered slot.

Remember this rule. Keeping a running figure across passes is a common chore. Create the figure before the loop begins, adjust it inside the body on every pass, and only trust its value once the loop has completely finished. It applies to every loop.
